messages.subject: Re: question on the ectotherm model in NicheMapR
messages.subject_clean: question on the ectotherm model in NicheMapR
messages.body_plain:
Dear Bingbing Liu,

Thanks for the question. There are a couple of things to note. First, for the cylinder shape, which you are using, I found a problem with the code for computing surface areas a couple of months which has now been fixed. The other thing is that the model had the behaviourally thermoregulating animal orienting itself perpendicular to the sun's rays to get warm if it was in the basking state. That isn't always going to be the case (esp. for some types of organisms that are more sessile or leaves which may or may not orient). The only way to stop that was to set 'LIVE=0' but that turned off all behaviour and metabolism. So I've just made some changes (pushed to github) such that when you set 'LIVE=2', it does all the behavioural thermoregulation and metabolism but doesn't orient to, or away from, the sun as part of thermoregulation. Your snakes, being cryptic sit-and-wait predators, probably choose their position mostly to maximise the chance of catching a bird and don't want to move around posturally and break their cover. So it would be might be more appropriate to set 'LIVE=2' in which case it will be in a posture that is in between perpendicular and parallel to the sun and isn't tilting toward the sun to be maximally absorbing solar radiation.

So if you run this code instead:
ecto<-ectotherm(Ww_g=Ww_g,
                T_F_min=T_F_min,
                T_F_max=T_F_max,
                T_B_min=T_B_min, #assume T_B_min=T_F_min
                T_RB_min=T_RB_min,
                T_pref=T_pref, #find the peak of the density plot of field body temperatures

                diurn=1,
                nocturn=1,
                crepus=1,
                climb=1,
                shape=1,

                postur=0,
                live=2,
                shape_b=15)

You could also play around with the microclimate model predictions, changing the slope, aspect, roughness height, and perhaps most importantly , change the height the microclimate simulation is using (input 'Usrhyt') because the default 1 cm height might be a bit too low for a big viper. You could also increase the default percent conduction (pct_cond = 10) to something more snakey. The microclimate simulation by default is for vegetation-covered ground (cap = 1, bulk density for loamy sand if I remember correctly). The thermal conductivity calculated by the microclimate model is used as the thermal conductivity the animal experiences for conductive heat flux. You could simulate the microclimate model with cap = 0 and change the BulkDensity (and BD vector) to be a little bit lower than the Density (and DD) vectors to simulate rock. Or you can use the code I've pasted below to simulate them on a more conductive surface (but which is at the same temperature as the predicted soil surface - this is not necessarily realistic because rock would not necessarily get as hot during the day as vegetation-covered surfaces where there's insulation from the veg preventing heat flowing into and out of the soil profile).

tcond <- micro$tcond # get the conductivity matrix out
tcond[, 3] <- 2.5 # change the conductivity of the 3rd column = soil surface to a value more like rock
ecto<-ectotherm(Ww_g=Ww_g,
                T_F_min=T_F_min,
                T_F_max=T_F_max,
                T_B_min=T_B_min, #assume T_B_min=T_F_min
                T_RB_min=T_RB_min,
                T_pref=T_pref, #find the peak of the density plot of field body temperatures

                diurn=1,
                nocturn=1,
                crepus=1,
                climb=1,
                shape=1,

                postur=0,
                live=2,
                shape_b=15,
                pct_cond = 40,
                tcond = tcond) # explicitly pass this modified conductivity vector in

Re the ibutton comparison, it seems like your times are out of alignment. If I add a couple of hours to the observed times I get a better alignment (so perhaps you haven't adjusted the GMT timezone correctly from the microclimate model output).

Finally, it looks like cloud came in on the day you presented Tb and ibutton data but the ERA5 microclimate prediction doesn't have this happen. That would also be an issue with the match between observations and predictions, but with the snakes you have them thermoregulating in the simulation making it look like they were in the field. It may, from the ibuttons, that they didn't need to in reality but they did in the simulation.

All the best,
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Hello guys,

May I have some help and advice, please...

I want to predict how a tree frog will react to changing temperatures and shade levels, that I can control.

I believe I would do this by inputting different temperatures, shade levels, cloud cover etc with a load of other parameters (that i do not necessarily care about) into the microclimate function and then using these results to run the ectotherm model but all I seem to do is wrong and I keep getting error messages, predominantly 'error: maxshades must be a vector with a length equal to the number of days simulated'

I am following instructions online for both models but I can not seem to find one that talks through running both at once, is there one or can someone help me on here?

I can happily share my R studios code if that will help or am I better off using the micro_global function? I have used this function using different coordinates with the ectotherm model and it works but can you specify the levels of shade or temperature within the micro_global function or is that determined by the coordinates I used?
(the micro_global and ectotherm help i have followed...... https://mrke.github.io/NicheMapR/inst/doc/ectotherm-model-tutorial)

Thank you so much for any help it is really appreciated as I am currently pulling out my hair, Ben

messages.subject: Re: help please:)
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

It's the same problem you had with the previous post in that you're passing the ectotherm model a vector of shade values that is less than the number of days being simulated. As I mentioned in response to the latter post, the ectotherm function is set up to make it easy to run if you've just run the microclimate model and returned the results to an object called 'micro'. But there's more work to do (and more traps) if you are trying to run it with a manual specification of the microclimate and you need to be careful and fully understand how it's using the microclimate info.

If you are just wanting to specify the microclimate and not calculated it, you would be better off using the ectoR_devel function, which has been in the package for a couple of years but hasn't been described in a publication yet. It just does a calculation for one combination of environmental conditions. Search for 'ectoR_devel' in the conversations for this google group and you'll find some info about it with examples. It's dated 11th Sept 2022. I think that might be a good place to start. The ectotherm function is ultimately faster and has a suite of behavioural options, but harder to wield in a customised manner without a fair bit of expertise in its idiosyncracies.

All the best,
Mike

messages.subject: Re: help please:)
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

If you want to use the micro_global function just to set up arbitrary environmental conditions for the ectotherm model, e.g. to simulate an experiment in the lab, with no behaviour, then you need to do something like this:

# to change all air, soil and sky temperatures to 20 deg C, relative humidity 50% and make wind all speed 0.1 m/s, solar radiation 100 W/m2 and shade 10% you'd do this:

micro <- micro_global() # run the model to get microclimate outputs to subsequently modify

metout <- micro$metout
soil <- micro$soil
head(metout) # see what columns each environmental factor is in
head(soil) # see which column is surface temp
metout[, 3] <- 20 # change local air temperature
metout[, 4] <- 20 # change reference air temperature
metout[, 5] <- 50 # change local relative humidity
metout[, 6] <- 50 # change reference  relative humidity (not really necessary)
metout[, 7] <- 0.1 # change local wind speed
metout[, 8] <- 0.1 # change reference wind speed (not really necessary)
metout[, 12] <- 0 # change solar zenith angle to 0
metout[, 13] <- 100 # change radiation to 100
metout[, 14] <- 20 # change sky temperature to 20
soil[, 3] <- 20 # change soil surface temps to 20
minshades <- micro$minshade * 0 + 10 # change minshades to 10%
ecto <- ectotherm(live = 0,
                  pct_wet = 80,
                  shape = 5,
                  metout = metout,
                  shadmet = metout,
                  soil = soil,
                  shadsoil = soil,
                  minshades = minshades)
environ <- as.data.frame(ecto$environ)
plot(environ$TC, type = 'l')

head(environ, 24)

You could of course make a range of combinations of conditions this way, e.g. make the first 10 local air temps temps 10, the next 10 air temps 15:

metout[1:10, 3] <- 10 # change local air temperature

metout[11:20, 3] <- 15 # change local air temperature

ecto <- ectotherm(live = 0,
                  pct_wet = 80,
                  shape = 5,
                  metout = metout,
                  shadmet = metout,
                  soil = soil,
                  shadsoil = soil,
                  minshades = minshades)
environ <- as.data.frame(ecto$environ)
plot(environ$TC, type = 'l')

head(environ, 24)

Note that setting live = 0 turns off metabolism and hence a small amount of metabolic heat, as well as respiratory water loss, but is a quick way to kill behaviour. You could alternatively turn off shade seeking, burrowing, make them active diurnally, nocturnally and crepuscularly, or make thresholds for activity extreme.

All the best,

Mike
